payload.throughline: Trace what an observer attends to and learns, predict whether modeled consequences change behavior, compare central and social-cognitive mechanisms, and vary the four packet-listed attitude-change factors.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Separate an observed model, the observer’s internal response, and the observer’s later behavior; the frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite lesson.
Starting observation: A child watches an adult sort recycling by label and later uses the same sorting rule without direct instruction. Which process is most directly shown?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: explain how observing another person can support learning or vicarious emotion while keeping model, consequence, cognition, and brain-process evidence distinct. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.

Modeling provides behavior and consequence information that an observer can attend to, retain, and later reproduce. Vicarious emotion occurs when observing another’s emotional state contributes to an observer’s own emotional response.

Mirror-neuron activity and other brain processes may contribute to mapping observed actions or states, but introductory evidence does not justify treating one neural mechanism as the complete explanation for imitation, empathy, or learning.
Use a five-link chain: model acts, consequence or emotion is visible, observer attends, an internal representation forms, and later response becomes possible.

I first ask what information was observable. Then I distinguish learning from performance: the observer may learn an action without immediately doing it. If neural evidence is supplied, I describe contribution rather than claiming a single brain system caused the whole behavior.
A novice watches a peer use a three-step equipment check and sees the peer prevent an error. Later, the novice performs the same check without direct instruction.
The case supports modeling and vicarious consequence information. It does not show that mirror neurons alone produced the behavior or that every observer will imitate.
Guided mechanism trace: mark the model action, observed consequence or emotion, observer attention, and later response.
Less support: choose a bounded modeling explanation from a fresh vignette.
On your own: separate observational learning from immediate imitation and from a sole-neural-mechanism claim.
Boundary: seeing an action does not guarantee attention, retention, ability, motivation, or performance, and correlated brain activity is not a complete causal account.
Near exit: explain a familiar modeled-action case using a bounded multi-link chain.
Changed exit: integrate a vicarious emotional response with supplied neural evidence without reducing the outcome to one mechanism.
Repair modeling: list only what the model did, what the observer could see, and what the observer later did; do not infer an unobserved sole cause.
Fresh re-entry: explain a new observed-action case with new people, behavior, and consequence.
Repair multi-mechanism reasoning: replace “caused entirely by” with a contribution statement and name the behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and neural evidence separately.
Fresh changed re-entry: select a bounded explanation for a new vicarious-emotion and brain-evidence vignette.
Recap: observational learning is a chain from model information to later response; vicarious and neural processes can contribute without becoming a single complete explanation.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the model, the observed behavior, the visible consequence, and the observer’s later opportunity to act.
Starting observation: A student sees a similar peer praised for showing work and can use the same method. What is the most bounded prediction?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: apply observational learning to one person’s behavior using model characteristics, observed consequences, and vicarious processes. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.
Observers are more likely to attend to models who are salient, credible, skilled, similar, or otherwise relevant in the vignette. Attention alone does not guarantee retention or performance.

Observed reward can increase expected value of a behavior; observed cost can reduce it. Capability, opportunity, self-expectation, and vicarious emotion can alter whether learned behavior is performed.
Use four prediction gates: NOTICE the model, VALUE the consequence, CAN perform, and GET an opportunity.
I compare each option with all four gates. A rewarded credible model can raise likelihood, but if the observer lacks the needed skill or opportunity, immediate performance may still be unlikely.
A novice watches a similar peer receive recognition for asking clarifying questions. The novice can ask the same questions and soon enters a comparable meeting.
Similarity, visible reward, capability, and opportunity align, so observational learning predicts an increased likelihood—not certainty—of asking questions.
Guided prediction: inventory model relevance, observed consequence, capability, and opportunity.
Less support: predict a fresh individual behavior from a modeled-consequence sequence.
On your own: avoid both certainty and a behavior-change program recommendation.
Boundary: a prestigious model may attract attention yet be hard to imitate; a punished behavior may still be learned even if not performed.
Near exit: predict behavior when model relevance and observed consequence align.
Changed exit: revise the prediction when capability or observed consequence changes.
Repair application: fill the four gates and make a directional likelihood claim only if the supplied conditions support it.
Fresh re-entry: predict behavior in a new modeled-action vignette.
Repair changed conditions: hold learned information constant, alter the named reward, cost, capability, or opportunity, and revise only performance likelihood.
Fresh changed re-entry: predict a bounded behavior shift after a new consequence change.
Recap: model relevance and vicarious consequences shape learning, while capability and opportunity help determine performance.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify whether the outcome is an attitude judgment, a performed behavior, or both, and list the message and social information supplied.
Starting observation: A highly involved audience has time and knowledge to compare evidence quality in a message. Which ELM route is most likely?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: contrast an elaboration-likelihood account of persuasion with a social-cognitive account of behavior and attitude change. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.

In the elaboration likelihood model, high motivation and ability favor central processing of argument quality. Low elaboration makes peripheral cues more influential. Central-route change is generally tied more closely to considered arguments; peripheral-cue effects may be more context dependent.

Social cognitive theory models reciprocal relations among personal factors, behavior, and environment. Observational learning and self-efficacy can influence whether a person attempts and sustains behavior.
Ask two different questions: ELM—how deeply is the message processed? Social cognitive—how do person, behavior, and environment influence one another?

If the case varies motivation, distraction, argument strength, or source cues, I test an ELM prediction. If it varies self-efficacy, modeled success, behavior feedback, or environmental opportunity, I test a social-cognitive prediction.
Two audiences receive the same strong arguments. One is highly involved and has time to evaluate them; the other is distracted and notices only an attractive spokesperson.
ELM predicts greater argument-quality sensitivity in the involved group and greater cue sensitivity in the distracted group. This does not require a social-cognitive behavior loop.
Guided model selection: classify the manipulated condition as elaboration, cue, self-efficacy, modeled behavior, or environment.
Less support: choose the model-consistent prediction in a fresh case.
On your own: contrast the two models without mixing their core premises.
Boundary: source characteristics can become arguments when relevant to the claim, and social cognitive theory is broader than imitation alone.
Near exit: select ELM or social cognitive theory for a familiar case and predict the outcome.
Changed exit: hold the message constant while changing elaboration or self-efficacy and compare model predictions.
Repair model selection: underline the changed variable and map it to message processing or a person-behavior-environment relation before predicting.
Fresh re-entry: select the model in a new persuasion or behavior vignette.
Repair contrast: write one ELM prediction tied to processing and one social-cognitive prediction tied to efficacy, modeling, behavior, or environment.
Fresh changed re-entry: generate the correct prediction after a new model-specific variable changes.
Recap: ELM predicts persuasion from elaboration and cues; social cognitive theory predicts change from reciprocal personal, behavioral, and environmental processes.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the attitude outcome and separate the behavior, message, target person, and social context variables in the case.
Starting observation: A study changes argument evidence while keeping audience and social setting constant. Which factor class changed?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.
Goal: predict attitude change by organizing evidence into behavior, message, target, and social factor classes. The frozen packet declares no hard prerequisite handoff for this lesson.

Behavior factors concern what a person has done or committed to. Message factors include argument quality, framing, repetition, and source properties only when supplied. Target factors include motivation, prior attitude, knowledge, need, and processing ability in the vignette.

Social factors include norms, group membership, modeled approval, and interpersonal context. Factors can interact, so a message can affect targets differently or a social norm can change how behavior is interpreted.
Use four boxes—DO, MESSAGE, PERSON, PEOPLE. Place each manipulated variable in one box before predicting.

I compare only the supplied levels and outcome. If the same message works better for highly involved targets, I name a target-by-message interaction rather than claiming one message is universally persuasive.
Two groups read the same strong argument. One group believes the issue affects an upcoming decision; the other sees no personal relevance.
Personal relevance is a target characteristic that can increase elaboration and attitude change. The message itself is held constant.
Guided factor map: classify the changed variable, hold the other three classes constant, and predict the bounded attitude difference.
Less support: identify the factor class in a fresh vignette.
On your own: interpret a simple factorial comparison without inventing a tactic or program.
Boundary: a source trait can be a message characteristic, while the audience’s prior belief is a target characteristic; group approval is social, not merely message content.
Near exit: classify one manipulated factor and predict the attitude result.
Changed exit: interpret an interaction between two factor classes in a small study.
Repair factor classification: ask whether the variable changes what the person did, what was communicated, who received it, or the surrounding social context.
Fresh re-entry: classify and apply a new factor with new content and targets.
Repair interaction reasoning: compare the message effect separately at each target or social level before stating where the difference changes.
Fresh changed re-entry: interpret a new two-factor attitude graph without generalizing beyond its cells.
Recap: behavior, message, target, and social factors each shape attitude change, and their effects may depend on one another.
